segments.say: Imagine you're walking down a busy corridor, and someone bumps into your shoulder. It's not hard, but it's noticeable. In the half second after it happens, your mind does something very quick. It decides what that bump meant. Was it an accident? Were they distracted? Or did they do it on purpose?

Here's the interesting thing. The bump itself is exactly the same either way. Same shoulder, same force, same corridor. But if you decide it was an accident, you probably shrug and walk on. If you decide it was deliberate, you might feel a flash of heat in your face. The feeling depends far more on the story than on the bump.

From around 1980, an American psychologist called Kenneth Dodge began studying exactly this kind of moment. He was especially interested in children, and in why some children got into fights much more often than others. And one of the things he looked at was how children read situations that could be understood in more than one way.

Think of the kind of moments that happen in a school every day. Someone knocks over your tower of blocks. Someone spills a drink on your drawing. Someone bumps you in the lunch queue. Often, it's genuinely unclear whether they meant it. It could easily have been an accident. So what does a child decide?

Dodge and others found that some children tended to read these unclear moments as hostile. They assumed the other child had done it on purpose, to be mean. Psychologists call this a hostile attribution bias. And children who read situations this way were more likely to respond with anger and aggression.

Now, this research started with children, but the idea is easy to recognise in adults too. The colleague who didn't reply to your email. The driver who didn't let you in. The friend who cancelled at the last minute. Each of these could be careless, or busy, or entirely innocent. But on some days, we jump straight to the hostile version.

Here's a simple way to put it. The feeling follows the story we tell. If the story is, they meant to hurt me, anger arrives quickly and easily. If the story is, they were probably just distracted, the anger has much less to hold on to. And very often, the story is something we've filled in ourselves.

show.text: The feeling follows the story we tell.
show.by: A simple way to put it

segments.say: Picture a phone lying on a table, next to a cup of tea and a pair of glasses. A message is waiting on it. There's no voice, no face, no smile, no sigh. Just words. And that brings us to a very modern version of this old problem.

When someone speaks to us in person, we get a lot of extra information. The tone of their voice. The look on their face. Whether they're smiling. Whether they sound tired, or worried, or teasing. All of that helps us read what they mean. But in a short text message, almost all of it disappears.

So what do we do instead? We fill in the gaps. And we tend to fill them in with whatever we're already feeling. If we're relaxed and happy, a short message sounds fine. If we're tired, hungry and frustrated, the very same message can sound cold, or critical, or even cruel.

So let's go back to those three words on Sam's phone. You forgot again? Here are some of the ways they could be read. As gentle teasing between brothers. As a little disappointment. As real hurt. Or as an attack, a way of saying, you always let me down. The words are exactly the same in every case.

And which reading did Sam choose, in that first split second on the bus? The last one. He heard an attack. He heard, you always let me down. And with that story in place, the anger arrived instantly, and so did the sharp reply. He didn't decide to read it that way. It just happened, the way these readings usually do.

Why that reading? Partly because of everything we've already seen. The tiredness, the hunger, the long day, the warm bus. When we're already frayed, the hostile reading simply fits better. It matches how we feel. And maybe partly because of history. If Sam has forgotten things before, it's easy for him to hear again as a kind of accusation.

But what if Sam's brother was actually just disappointed? Or worried? Or even trying to be a bit funny about it? What if he was tired too? We don't know. And that's the point. In the moment, Sam doesn't know either. He's reacting to a story he's written himself, in half a second, with the help of a long and difficult day.

This is where one of the simplest and most useful questions in the psychology of anger comes in. It isn't a complicated technique. It's just a question you can ask yourself, quietly, before you reply. Is there another way to read this?

Asking that question doesn't mean pretending that nobody ever means harm. Sometimes they do. Sometimes the hostile reading is the right one. But very often, it isn't. And just taking a moment to consider another reading can be enough to let some of the heat out, before it turns into words we can't take back.

Here are a few gentle questions that can help. Is there another way to read this? What would I think if I'd read this on a good day? Could they be tired, or busy, or worried too? And perhaps the kindest one of all. If I'd sent this message, how would I want them to read it?

show.title: Questions that help
items: What would I think on a good day?
What would I want them to assume about me?

segments.say: That last question is a small act of fairness. We usually know our own intentions. When we send a short message, we know we meant it kindly, or quickly, or with a tired smile. But other people can't see that. So giving them the same benefit of the doubt we'd want for ourselves is often the fairest reading of all.

Sam hasn't asked himself any of these questions yet. He's still on the bus, still holding his phone, still feeling the heat in his face. But the reading he chose isn't the only possible one. And somewhere in the back of his mind, a quieter voice might already be wondering whether his brother really meant it the way it sounded.

Before we follow that quieter voice, though, let's look more closely at some of the hidden ingredients that made the hostile reading so easy tonight. Because Sam skipped lunch. And one of the most charming studies in the whole psychology of anger involves married couples, blood sugar, and a little doll full of pins.
